title: Prayer: Part 5 - For Whom and What Should We Pray?
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro
summary: This lesson addresses two fundamental questions about Christian prayer: for whom should we pray, and what should we pray for? Using the Larger Catechism as a guide, Pastor Lyro explores the biblical priorities for prayer, including the whole Church of Christ, civic leaders and ministers, ourselves, our brethren, our enemies, and all people, while explaining what we should not pray for (the dead and those who commit the sin unto death). The lesson emphasizes that all prayers must tend toward God's glory and be grounded in Scripture.

outline.title: The Foundation of Christian Prayer
subpoints: Christian prayer is Trinitarian, involving the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit
Prayer must align with biblical priorities, not personal preferences
Scripture study and prayer must go hand in hand

outline.title: For Whom We Should Pray: The Whole Church of Christ
subpoints: Pray for the universal Church, not just your local congregation
The Church is one body under Christ as the head
We must be informed about the global Church to pray effectively for it
Direct command found in the Lord's Prayer: 'Your kingdom come'

outline.title: For Whom We Should Pray: Civic Leaders and Ministers
subpoints: Direct command to pray for kings and all in authority
Prayer for leaders affects the peacefulness and godliness of our lives
Pray for salvation, blessing on families, and righteous leadership
Ministers and magistrates need wisdom, courage, honesty, and integrity through intercessory prayer

outline.title: For Whom We Should Pray: Ourselves and Our Brethren
subpoints: We are commanded to pray for ourselves, including spiritual and temporal needs
Prayer for ourselves must not be selfish; it must submit to God's will
Pray for spiritual blessings like growth in Christ and sanctification
Pray for the unity and welfare of church members

outline.title: For Whom We Should Pray: Our Enemies
subpoints: Direct command to love, bless, and pray for those who persecute us
Having enemies is inevitable; even Christ had enemies
Praying for enemies does not prevent us from defending ourselves
This applies to all relationships, including marriage

outline.title: For Whom We Should Not Pray
subpoints: Do not pray for the dead; their eternal state is fixed
Do not pray for those known to have committed the sin unto death
The sin unto death is likely the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit
It represents stubborn, permanent resistance to the Holy Spirit

outline.title: What We Should Pray For
subpoints: Pray for all things that tend to God's glory
Pray for the welfare of the Church as the bride of Christ
Pray for our own sanctification and spiritual growth
Pray for the good of others, their salvation, and temporal blessings
Do not pray about things the Bible has already forbidden

transcript:
## The Foundation of Christian Prayer

I'm so thankful that there are men and women who have gone before us who are smarter than me and able to think through things and organize them in a very helpful way. That's what we find with the Larger Catechism. As we've been talking about prayer, we saw what prayer is. In the first lesson, the question and answer sets out the other questions and answers regarding prayer. Then we saw that prayer should only be offered to the God of the Bible. There's no other God that would listen and hear prayer, so we're not offering prayers to saints or to trees or to Buddha or any other god except the God of the Bible.

Then we saw that prayers can only be offered in Jesus' name because of what His name represents—not necessarily as a formula, but as representing faith in who He is and what He's done. Last week, we saw that the Holy Spirit helps us when we pray, and when we put all this together, we see that Christian prayer is Trinitarian. It involves the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and each one has a function in that.

The Catechism takes us today to the content of our prayers—both the subjects of our prayers and the content, the things we pray for. That's what we're going to be looking at today. But we're going to start with a real question: whom should we pray for? It's an important one. It's not a hard question, but it's important that we put the same priority in our prayers that the Bible puts in our prayers as far as whom we're praying for. Sometimes we may be surprised as to what the Bible emphasizes and how it's reflected in our prayers.

Do you realize that there's no direct command to pray for unsaved family members? That's not found anywhere in the Bible. It's implied in different things, but there's no direct command. Yet when you hear our prayers, you'd think that was the first command made. Do you know there's a direct command to pray for your political leaders? Yet when you hear our prayers, there's not a lot of that. There's a direct command to pray for missions. Yet when we hear our prayers, it doesn't seem to reflect that as much. So it's important that when we think of whom we should pray for, we put the same emphasis that the Scriptures put on that.

## For Whom Are We to Pray?

Question 183 of the Larger Catechism asks, "For whom are we to pray?" And it answers: "We are to pray for the whole Church of Christ upon earth, for magistrates and ministers, for ourselves, our brethren, our enemies, and for all sorts of men living or that shall live hereafter, but not for the dead, nor for those that are known to have sinned the sin unto death."

You can see that it didn't take highly intelligent people to write this. We could have done that, but did we know that this is the emphasis of the Scriptures? Could we have done it without seeing it written or spoken? Often we see something and say, "Oh, that's obvious," but until we had seen it written or spoken, we would not be able to formulate that obvious thing. So let's look at each category.

### The Whole Church of Christ Upon Earth

The first thing is that we must pray for the whole Church of Christ on earth because of the spiritual unity of the Church as one body under Christ the head. Do we have examples of that being done in the Bible? Can you think of examples of someone praying for the whole Church? Yes, Christ prayed for the whole Church in John 17.

> "Father, the hour has come. Glorify Your Son, that Your Son also may glorify You." (John 17:1)

We also see this in Ephesians 3, and are we directly commended to pray for the whole Church? Yes. Remember, what's the second petition of the Lord's Prayer? The first one is, "Hallowed be Your name." The second one is, "Your kingdom come." We're praying for the whole Church of Christ there. That means that we are not to limit our prayers to the branch of the Church of which we ourselves are members. We're praying for the Church in general.

That also implies that we need to be informed about what's going on in the Church in general in order to be able to pray for it. We don't need to know everything that's going on everywhere, but we need to know enough to care and to pray for other churches. I try to instill that in our worship service when I pray for other churches, at least in our area, who are also proclaiming the Gospel of Jesus Christ. But the Church is not limited to this area, to this state, to this country. It's all over the world. It's important that we remember that we have a direct command to pray for the whole Kingdom of God, not just the neighborhood of our Kingdom of God in which we find ourselves.

### Magistrates and Ministers

We are also commanded to pray for our civic leaders and ministers and all in positions of authority in both state and church. In 1 Timothy 2, Paul says:

> "Therefore I exhort first of all that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks be made for all men, for kings and all who are in authority, that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and reverence." (1 Timothy 2:1-2)

This is of most importance, much like he says in 1 Corinthians 15 that something is of "first importance." If you're not living a peaceful life, if your life is not godly, one of the things you should ask yourself is: am I praying for those who have authority over me? Because here Paul says that one of the ways that you live a peaceable and godly life is by praying for those who have the authority over you.

One example of a request for prayer for ministers is Paul himself. He does that also in Ephesians and Colossians 4:3-4:

> "Meanwhile, praying also for us, that God would open to us a door for the word, to speak the mystery of Christ, for which I am also in chains, that I may make it manifest as I ought to speak." (Colossians 4:3-4)

You find almost every epistle in the New Testament contains a request by the author, by the minister who is writing it, asking the church to pray for the ministry of the word of God. In 2 Timothy, Paul says, "Look, I'm in prison, but the word of God is not chained." He wants prayer for the ministry of the word of God.

Both the state and the church are divine institutions for the accomplishment of God's purposes in the world. Both the magistrate, which is a civil leader, and the minister need wisdom, courage, honesty, and integrity, in addition to all kinds of gifts from God that come through the prayers of God's people. If you think the civil government is not doing well, one of the ways to minister to them is by praying for them—prayers of blessing. We should pray that the Lord would remove the wicked and replace them with the righteous. But also we need to pray for the salvation of our political leaders and for blessings upon their families, that they will lead us in righteousness.

If you're dissatisfied with the ministry of the church, the ministry of the church is not singled out in the minister, but one of the ways to better that is by praying for your pastor—hopefully not in imprecatory prayers either.

### Ourselves

Is there a direct command to pray for ourselves? Yes. Jesus Himself prayed for His own well-being. One example is in John 17 where He says:

> "Father, the hour has come. Glorify Your Son, that Your Son also may glorify You." (John 17:1, 5)

We also pray for ourselves in the fourth, fifth, and sixth petitions of the Lord's Prayer:

> "Give us this day our daily bread. Forgive us our debts as we forgive our debtors. Do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil." (Matthew 6:11-13)

So it's appropriate to pray for ourselves. As a matter of fact, we must pray for ourselves. We have to be careful though that these prayers are not selfish. In James 4:3, James says:

> "You ask and do not receive, because you ask amiss, that you may spend it on your pleasures." (James 4:3)

There's a selfish way to pray for ourselves. We may pray for legitimate temporal blessings for ourselves, such as health or healing. We can pray that the Lord will provide food, clothing, material prosperity, success in business, and the list just goes on. God will give us these blessings in answer to our prayers so far as it is in accordance with His glory and our own true welfare.

That's why one of the petitions of the Lord's Prayer is, "Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven." That guides all our prayers. And that's a measure of an unselfish prayer—when you can ask whatever from the Lord and at the end you can say, "But Your will be done, whatever that is," and then be satisfied with that.

We also ought to pray for spiritual blessings for ourselves. When we do that sincerely and humbly, we can be confident that God will answer our prayers either by granting our requests for whatever spiritual growth we're asking, or in some other way that is even better according to His own wisdom and love.

### Our Brethren

We're also supposed to pray for our brethren. Are there direct examples or commands to pray for our brethren in the Bible? Yes. We see this in Ephesians. Paul prays for the churches, and you find that in every epistle—in 1 Thessalonians, in Ephesians several times in chapters 1 and 3. But in every letter he prays for the church there. And in Ephesians 4, we're called to pray for unity of the church. In every letter Paul prays for the churches.

### Our Enemies

And then it says that we are to pray for our enemies, and there are direct commands for that as well.

> "I say to you, love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who spitefully use you and persecute you." (Matthew 5:44)

You can see again, these are not prayers of implication for their destruction, because it starts with the idea of blessing them. Paul also says in Romans 12:14:

> "Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse." (Romans 12:14)

In 1 Corinthians 4:12, Paul experiences that and practices it:

> "Being reviled, we bless. Being persecuted, we endure." (1 Corinthians 4:12)

The word "reviled" means to be verbally abused. So when Paul was abused, his reaction was to bless.

What is the implication of this command to pray for enemies? The implication is that we're going to have enemies. It's a given in life. Jesus Himself, the perfect one, had enemies, and we are not perfect. We're around people who are not perfect. Even if we behave ourselves above reproach, people are still going to be upset with us, and we are to pray for them.

This can be a great thing regarding family relationships. Sometimes you might see your spouse as your enemy, and you might be tempted to revile against them or be mean to them. But even if you see your spouse as your enemy, the command in the Bible is to pray for them and to love them. So we can't get out of that—we're called to love them and pray for God's blessing upon them.

Now, praying for them does not mean that we can't resist their attacks. If you're in war and you pray for your enemy, it doesn't mean that when they attack you, you just don't shoot back. That's not the point. You can shoot and pray. Hopefully you can chew gum and walk at the same time. That's consistent with the whole of the Scriptures.

### All People Living and to Come

And then we are to pray for people who are living and who will live. We have to pray for everyone. That's the idea—we pray for people who are living and who will live. We saw already that in 2 Timothy, where Paul says that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks be made for all men. This is a general word for all people. We can pray.

Jesus Himself did that in John 17:

> "I do not pray for these alone, but also for those who will believe in Me through their word." (John 17:20)

That's a prayer for us that He prayed 2,000 years ago. So Jesus prayed for us and He continues to pray for us before the throne of God.

## For Whom We Should NOT Pray

### The Dead

But the Catechism says that we are not to pray for the dead. The reason is that the dead have their state fixed—they're either in heaven or they're in hell. So there's no point in praying for them. Hebrews 9:27 says:

> "It is appointed for men to die once, but after this the judgment." (Hebrews 9:27)

Once you die, that's it. There's no changing there, so there's no purpose for praying there. The idea of praying for the dead arose from the doctrine of purgatory, which teaches that souls that don't do enough on earth to go to heaven can go there to finish paying for their sins. The doctrine also teaches that people that are still alive can atone, can do stuff to help those people get out of purgatory. That's where this idea of praying for the dead came from, at least in Christian circles. It's very common in pagan circles to be praying for the dead or to pray that your dead ancestors will bless you. It's very common in Japanese pagan culture where ancestor worship is a big deal. But the Bible teaches that once you die, that's it. There's no second chance—it's either hell or heaven. Therefore, there's no point in praying there.

### Those Who Have Committed the Sin Unto Death

The Catechism also says that we are not to pray for those who have committed the sin unto death. That's a reference to 1 John 5:16, where John says:

> "If anyone sees his brother sinning a sin which does not lead to death, he will ask, and He will give him life for those who commit sin not leading to death. There is sin leading to death. I do not say that he should pray about that." (1 John 5:16)

Theologians believe that there's some agreement that the sin unto death may be the same as the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit that you find in the synoptic Gospels. For example, in Matthew 12:31, Jesus says:

> "I say to you, every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven men, but the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven." (Matthew 12:31)

As we look at the whole of the Scriptures and see that this sin is unforgivable, it's not because it is too great to be forgiven, but because the one who commits it has no desire to repent of it. That's why there's no point in praying for the person, because they're not going to repent. They have no desire to repent.

Theologians understand this sin to be a stubborn, permanent, and complete resistance to the pleadings of the Holy Spirit, which ultimately results in the Holy Spirit abandoning the person to his own sin and ceasing to influence him—a removal of the spirit from influencing that person.

We should not pray for a person who is known to have sinned the sin unto death because that prayer will not be answered. We should, however, be extremely cautious about saying that a particular individual has sinned the sin unto death. The Bible is not clear on how to recognize this sin. If there is any reasonable doubt as to whether a person committed the sin unto death, we should pray for them.

There may be a correlation to Hebrews 6, where we have somebody who professed faith in Christ, who experienced all the blessings of being in Christ as far as being the Church of the Lord Jesus Christ, and yet at that point denied Christ in an active way. There it says it's impossible for that person to repent. So maybe this is all talking about the same thing—an abject denial of Christ and becoming an evangelist for that denial, not just somebody denying it, but becoming an evangelist for that, trying to deceive others that way. So those could all be related.

Based on the explanation given, the reason the sin unto death is more of a continuously observable state that we see someone in, or are we looking for evidence of one specific action? It could be both. It could be either, I should say. It could be either because it does talk about the singular, the sin and the death, but it could manifest itself over time as well.

## What Should We Pray For?

Now the question becomes, what should we pray for? Question 184 helps us with that. It asks, "For what things are we to pray?" The answer is: "We are to pray for all things tending to the glory of God, the welfare of the church, our own or others' good, but not for any unlawful things."

The most important consideration in figuring out what to pray for is the glory of God. Is this going to bring glory to God? And the only way to know if something tends or leads to God's glory is by studying the Scriptures. Prayer and Scripture study go together hand in hand. We can't pray rightly if we don't know the Bible rightly. It doesn't mean, however, that unless you have a seminary degree, you can't pray. It means that you're going to search the Scriptures to see what it is that brings glory to God.

We have to pray for the welfare of the church because it is the bride of Christ. I wonder how much time we spend praying for the church and things about the church. One example of that is Psalm 51:18 where the Psalmist said:

> "Do good in Your good pleasure to Zion; build the walls of Jerusalem." (Psalm 51:18)

As you trace the use of Zion and Jerusalem, you're going to see that that's an application to the church of Jesus Christ. And one of the reasons why we had to pray for all things for the church is that as goes the church, so goes everything else. But we've put so little emphasis on corporate life as believers that we don't really care about the church. Everything gets in the way of church. We are fine with not seeing each other. We are okay with just being ourselves independently from one another. Yet life in the Bible is a corporate life. The unit in the Bible is not the individual; it's the family and the church. We forget that.

We pray for the well-being of the visible church, not just our group but all that are involved in worshiping Christ.

### Praying for Our Own Good

We also pray for what is good for us, our own good. We see that in Matthew 7 where the Lord says:

> "Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and he who seeks finds, and to him who knocks it will be opened. Or what man is there among you who, if his son asks for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will he give him a serpent? If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask Him?" (Matthew 7:7-11)

So we know that what the Scriptures say is good for us is good for us. We pray for our sanctification. We pray that we would grow in Christ. We pray that we would become more like the Lord Jesus Christ. We pray that we would die to sin and live unto righteousness. And we pray for other things also according to God's will.

### Praying for the Good of Others

Besides praying for ourselves, we pray also for the good of others. We pray for their salvation. We pray for temporal blessings for the glory of God to come upon them.

### What We Should NOT Pray For

But we will not pray for anything that goes against the word of God. If the Bible forbids something, we don't need to pray about it. For example, you're interested in a man or a woman, a boy or a girl, and they're not a believer, and you're going to pray whether you should date them or not. You don't have to. You already have that answer. The answer is no. Because you're not supposed to marry them, therefore you're not supposed to be in a relationship with them, as they're supposed to lead to marriage. Does it make sense?

So the Bible forbids that. Then you just don't need to pray. You already have the answer right there. But you need to know the Bible in order to be able to do that.

You don't need to pray whether you should look at pornography or not. The Bible already says don't. You don't need to pray whether you should have an affair or any emotional affair, whatever. The Bible already says no. You don't need to pray whether you should raise your children in the nurture and admonition of the Lord. The Bible already says that. You pray for the grace to do so, not whether you should do it. Does it make sense?

You can see again that we need to know the Bible in order to pray appropriate prayers. So here we have these two questions that tell us whom we should pray for and what we should pray for—those groups that are in the red letters in our slides. So let's close in prayer.
